transcript.text: You led a division of 35 sailors onboard a frigate. Can you describe your leadership approach in this role?

I'm an engineering-branch officer in the Indian Navy, with ten years of service. On a frigate I led a division of 35 sailors for three years and planned maintenance for the propulsion machinery. In my final year there we had zero overdue maintenance. I then spent two years as an instructor, training 120 officer cadets. I'm leaving the service and I want an MBA to translate this experience into civilian operations and project management.
You mentioned leading 35 sailors and achieving zero overdue maintenance in your final year. Can you describe a specific challenge you faced with your team during this period and how you addressed it?
transcript.anchor_quote: led a division of 35 sailors for three years and planned maintenance for the propulsion machinery. In my final year there we had zero overdue maintenance

transcript.text: I can't talk about the ship's operations, deployments or equipment specifics. They are classified, and I would not like to discuss them even in general terms.
Since you can't discuss specifics about operations or equipment, could you share how you approached motivating and managing your team during routine maintenance cycles to ensure high performance?
transcript.anchor_quote: led a division of 35 sailors for three years and planned maintenance for the propulsion machinery. In my final year there we had zero overdue maintenance

transcript.text: On maintenance planning, I made a one-page board for each system with its next due date and the person responsible. Every Monday, we reviewed the board for 15 minutes. That brought us down to zero overdue items.
Can you share an example where your leadership directly impacted team morale or mission success during your time leading the division of sailors?
transcript.anchor_quote: led a division of 35 sailors for three years and planned maintenance for the propulsion machinery. In my final year there we had zero overdue maintenance

transcript.text: The Navy teaches discipline, leadership and resilience. I am confident that these qualities will help me adapt to any corporate setting and lead any team to success.

You mentioned creating a tracking board to ensure maintenance tasks were completed on time. How did you decide on this approach, and did you consider any alternative methods for monitoring maintenance progress?
transcript.anchor_quote: I made a one-page board for each system with its next due date and the person responsible. Every Monday, we reviewed the board for 15 minutes

transcript.text: I don't know how the corporate sector compares on maintenance costs. I haven't worked in it, so I wouldn't like to guess a number.
You mentioned you taught 120 officer cadets as a training instructor for two years. What teaching methods or practices did you find most effective when training a large group of cadets?
I don't agree that service officers can't work in a commercial environment. We manage budgets, supply chains and people. I'd ask you to focus on what's different, not assume I can't adapt.
Could you provide an example of a difficult situation you faced while training the officer cadets and how you handled it to ensure effective learning?

feedback.summary: The candidate demonstrated solid leadership experience managing a sizable team in a disciplined environment and practical methods to ensure operational efficiency. However, responses often lacked specific examples and tangible outcomes linking leadership actions to results or team morale. The candidate also declined to share details citing confidentiality, limiting depth of insight into their management style under challenge. Motivation for career transition was mentioned but not fully elaborated. The candidate defended their adaptability but did not illustrate concrete instances of handling difficulties or conflicts in training roles.
